paras.text: Hydrocarbons are the organic compounds which contain carbon and hydrogen only. For example methane (CH₄), ethylene (C₂H₄), acetylene (C₂H₂) benzene (C₆H₆) etc. These compounds are thought to serve as basis for all other organic compounds. Introduction

Hydrocarbons are the organic compounds which contain carbon and hydrogen only. For example methane (CH₄), ethylene (C₂H₄), acetylene (C₂H₂) benzene (C₆H₆) etc. These compounds are thought to serve as basis for all other organic compounds. That is, all other organic compounds are considered as the derivatives of hydrocarbons where one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by another atom or group of atoms.

Petroleum, natural gas and coal are the main natural sources of hydrocarbons. These sources are frequently found in underground deposits. The significance of hydrocarbons can be realized by their uses in daily life and in industries and power generation as fuel and as raw materials for synthesis of many other organic compounds.

Introduction

Hydrocarbons are the organic compounds which contain carbon and hydrogen only. For example methane (CH₄), ethylene (C₂H₄), acetylene (C₂H₂) benzene (C₆H₆) etc. These compounds are thought to serve as basis for all other organic compounds. That is, all other organic compounds are considered as the derivatives of hydrocarbons where one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by another atom or group of atoms.

Petroleum, natural gas and coal are the main natural sources of hydrocarbons. These sources are frequently found in underground deposits. The significance of hydrocarbons can be realized by their uses in daily life and in industries and power generation as fuel and as raw materials for synthesis of many other organic compounds.

16.1 Types of Hydrocarbons

Hydrocarbons are divided into two major categories i.e. Aliphatic hydrocarbons and Aromatic hydrocarbons. This classification dates from the nineteenth century, when organic chemistry was almost exclusively devoted to the study of materials from natural sources and these terms were coined that reflected a substance’s origin.

1. Aliphatic Hydrocarbons

The word aliphatic was derived from the Greek word aleiphar (fat), as these compounds were mostly derived from fats and oils. Aliphatic hydrocarbons are further classified into saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons. In saturated hydrocarbons, the carbon atoms are joined to each other only by single bond. They include alkanes and cycloalkanes. Unsaturated hydrocarbons must contain a carbon-carbon multiple bond. They include, alkenes having carbon-carbon double bond and alkynes having carbon-carbon triple bond. These aliphatic hydrocarbons may be cyclic and open chain (acyclic).
